passage: Thursday Lakshmi asked me "Is this right, Sir?" eleven times during one maths lesson. I counted. Her eyes filled up when I said, "You already know it is." She hardly speaks at break, just stands near the classroom door. I nearly said "Stop worrying" again. It didn't help last week. Instead, at the end of the day I sat beside her and asked quietly, "What's the scariest part of maths for you?" She whispered, "Getting it wrong and Amma being sad." I called her mother tonight. We agreed on a plan: Lakshmi gets two check-in cards a lesson; after those, she has a go on her own. At home they'll try the same. She's a kind, careful child. I want her to feel safe, not rescued every minute. - Akash

qa.q: How many times did Lakshmi ask 'Is this right, Sir?' in one lesson?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: How does Akash feel about Lakshmi when he writes that he wants her to feel safe?
qa.a: He feels caring and concerned for her, and wants her to feel safe rather than rescued every minute, which is why he stopped saying 'Stop worrying'.

qa.q: What plan did Akash agree on with Lakshmi's mother?
qa.a: Lakshmi gets two check-in cards a lesson and then has a go on her own, with the same idea at home.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel about having two check-in cards a lesson?
qa.a: Lakshmi may feel nervous at first about trying alone, but safer knowing she still has two chances to check.

grounding: A teacher notices a child seeking constant reassurance and tearful, uses gentle questions and a calm tone, and makes a plan with the family that neither dismisses nor feeds the worry.

passage: Since his father left for work in the city, eight-year-old Manoj had grown very quiet. At the village well, at the shop, at night, he asked Jaya the same thing: "Will Papa come back? What if he doesn't?" At first she said, "Of course he will, don't ask again." He asked twice as often. Then one evening, while shelling peas on the step, she asked softly, "What makes you think he won't?" Manoj's lip wobbled. "Raju's father went and never came." Jaya put the peas down. She didn't laugh or scold. She called his father on the phone that night, and his teacher the next day. Together they made a calendar on the kitchen wall with call days ticked in red and the day Papa comes home circled. Each morning Manoj ticked one box himself.

qa.q: What did Jaya and Manoj make on the kitchen wall?
qa.a: A calendar with call days ticked in red and the day Papa comes home circled.

qa.q: Why was Manoj so worried his father wouldn't come back?
qa.a: Raju's father went to work away and never came back, so Manoj feared the same.

qa.q: Which change in Jaya's approach helped?
qa.a: She stopped brushing off his question and asked gently what made him think so, then made a plan with his father and teacher.

qa.q: What might it be like for Manoj to tick a box on the calendar himself each morning?
qa.a: It likely makes him feel calmer and more in control, because he can see the calls and the day Papa comes home getting closer.

grounding: An adult notices a child who is quiet and constantly seeks reassurance, asks gentle questions, and makes a plan with the family and teacher.

passage: In a Prague primary school, Jana noticed that Ada, eight, asked "Is this right?" after every single sum, sometimes six times a lesson. Twice this week her eyes had filled with tears over a small mistake. At break Jana sat beside her. "You seem worried a lot lately. What's it like?" Ada whispered, "What if I get everything wrong and Mama is sad?" Jana kept her voice soft. "That sounds heavy. Thank you for telling me." That afternoon she phoned Ada's parents. They agreed together: Ada would get a star card to check her work herself, Jana would check in once each lesson, not every sum, and her parents would ask about her day, not her marks.

qa.q: How many times a lesson did Ada sometimes ask "Is this right?"
qa.a: She sometimes asked it six times a lesson.

qa.q: How did Jana feel about the pattern she noticed in Ada?
qa.a: Jana felt concerned and caring, noticing the constant questions and tears and choosing to gently ask about them.

qa.q: Why was the plan with Ada's parents a wise approach?
qa.a: It took the worry seriously without dismissing it, and reduced constant reassurance so it would not feed the worry.

qa.q: How might Ada feel about the star card plan?
qa.a: Ada may feel calmer and more capable, checking her own work and trusting a warm check-in instead of constant reassurance.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a child who is tearful and constantly seeking reassurance, using gentle questions, a calm tone and a plan with the family.

passage: At the swimming club, coach Vaibhav noticed Hafsa, ten, sitting silent on the bench while the others splashed. Before every session she asked, "Will I drown? Are you sure? Are you sure?" Last week she had cried in the changing room. He didn't say "Don't be silly," and he didn't let her skip forever. He crouched beside her. "You look worried. What's the scariest part?" "The deep end," she said. He nodded slowly. "That's a real feeling. Thanks for telling me." At pickup he spoke with her mother. They agreed: shallow end only for two weeks, the same warm-up every time, and Hafsa could hold the rail whenever she liked. Next session she slid in first.

qa.q: What did Hafsa say was the scariest part?
qa.a: She said the deep end was the scariest part.

qa.q: How did coach Vaibhav feel seeing Hafsa silent on the bench?
qa.a: He seemed concerned and gentle, noticing her worry and crouching down to ask about it calmly.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav avoid both dismissing and feeding Hafsa's worry?
qa.a: He did not call her silly or let her skip forever; he listened, then made a small, steady plan with her mother.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel about starting in the shallow end?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel safer and braver, which shows when she slides in first at the next session.

grounding: Shows an adult noticing a quiet, tearful child who keeps seeking reassurance, responding with gentle questions, a calm tone and a plan with the family.

passage: I'm Kishore, Tejas's Mama; I've lived with my sister's family since spring. For the last few weeks Tejas, nine, has been very quiet at dinner. He asks, "Mummy is definitely coming home at seven? Definitely?" three or four times a night. On Sunday I found him crying on the stairs, but he said nothing was wrong. I can't know what he's thinking. I didn't say "Stop worrying," and I didn't keep promising either. I sat down and said, "Something seems to be bothering you. I'm here." He leaned on my arm. That night I told my sister what I'd seen, and we arranged to meet his class teacher together on Tuesday to make a plan.

qa.q: What time does Tejas keep asking about?
qa.a: He keeps asking whether Mummy is definitely coming home at seven.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel finding Tejas crying on the stairs?
qa.a: Kishore felt concerned and tender, choosing to sit quietly with him rather than dismiss or feed the worry.

qa.q: What steps did Kishore take that were wise?
qa.a: He spoke calmly and gently, stayed with Tejas, told his sister that night and planned a meeting with the class teacher.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when he leaned on Kishore's arm?
qa.a: He may have felt comforted and safe, even if he couldn't yet say what was wrong.

grounding: Shows an adult relative noticing a quiet, tearful child seeking reassurance, responding gently and making a plan with the family and school.

passage:
Monday. Rashmi Ma'am noticed Pranav hadn't answered a single question all day. At lunch, he asked her three times, "Will my mother come at 2:30? Are you sure?" His eyes filled when the bell rang.
Wednesday. She didn't tell him "Don't be silly," but she didn't keep repeating "yes" either. She sat beside him and asked in a soft voice, "What's the worry that comes at lunch?" Pranav whispered that last month his mother had been late and he'd waited alone in the office.
Friday. Rashmi Ma'am met his parents after school. Together they made a plan: a card in his pocket with the pickup time, one check with the teacher at lunch, not five, and a promise that someone would always wait with him. Pranav held the card all through maths, but he answered two questions.

qa.q: What time did Pranav keep asking about?
What was Rashmi Ma'am feeling when she chose her words on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt concerned and careful, wanting to take his worry seriously without either dismissing it or feeding it with endless reassurance.

qa.q: Which of Rashmi Ma'am's steps would help other adults noticing a worried child?
qa.a: A gentle question in a calm voice to find the cause, then a clear plan made with the family, like the pickup card and one lunchtime check.

qa.q: What is it like for Pranav as the end of the day approaches?
qa.a: He feels anxious and sad, afraid of waiting alone again, which is why he keeps asking.

grounding: Rashmi Ma'am notices a quiet, tearful child seeking reassurance, asks gently and makes a plan with his family without dismissing or feeding the worry.
